questions.prompt: A model scores 99% accuracy on a dataset where 99% of rows are the negative class. What does that tell you?

options.text: The model is excellent
The model may be no better than always predicting the majority class
The model has overfitted the test set
The data must be corrupted

questions.explanation: With that imbalance a constant predictor also scores 99%. Precision, recall or AUC are needed to tell whether the model learned anything about the rare class.

questions.prompt: What is data leakage in a machine learning pipeline?

options.text: Information from outside the training window influencing the model
Exposing personal data in a report
Losing rows during a database export
Memory growing during training

questions.explanation: Fitting a scaler on the whole dataset before splitting, or using a feature computed after the target event, gives excellent validation scores and a model that fails in production.

questions.prompt: What does the bias-variance tradeoff describe?

options.text: The tension between underfitting and overfitting
The balance between training time and accuracy
The ratio of features to rows
The imbalance between classes

questions.explanation: High bias means the model is too simple to capture the signal; high variance means it fits noise in the training data. Reducing one usually increases the other.

questions.prompt: Why is a validation set kept separate from the test set?

options.text: Validation data is always larger
Validation data does not need labels
The test set trains the final model
Tuning against the test set makes its score optimistic

questions.explanation: Choosing hyperparameters using a set means you have fitted to it. The test set stays untouched so it remains an honest estimate of unseen performance.

questions.prompt: In SQL, what does a LEFT JOIN return that an INNER JOIN does not?

options.text: Duplicate rows removed automatically
Rows sorted by the join key
Only rows present in both tables
Rows from the left table with no match on the right

questions.explanation: Unmatched left rows are kept with NULLs for right columns. Filtering those NULL columns in WHERE silently turns the query back into an inner join.

questions.prompt: What does a p-value of 0.03 mean in a hypothesis test at the 5% level?

options.text: Data this extreme would occur 3% of the time if the null were true
The effect size is 3%
There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
The result will replicate 97% of the time

questions.explanation: The p-value is the probability of the data given the null, not the probability of the null given the data. It also says nothing about how large or important the effect is.

questions.prompt: Why is cross-validation preferred over a single train-test split on a small dataset?

options.text: It guarantees higher accuracy
It removes the need for a test set
It trains the model faster
Every row is used for validation once, giving a more stable estimate

questions.explanation: A single small split gives an estimate that swings with which rows landed where. K-fold averages across folds, at k times the training cost.

questions.prompt: What does regularisation such as L2 do to a model?

options.text: Normalises features to zero mean
Balances the class distribution
Removes duplicate rows before training
Penalises large coefficients to reduce overfitting

questions.explanation: Adding a penalty on coefficient magnitude discourages the model from fitting noise. L1 can drive coefficients to exactly zero, which also performs feature selection.

questions.prompt: When is recall more important than precision?

options.text: When false alarms are very costly
When the model is a regression
When missing a positive case is very costly
When the classes are perfectly balanced

questions.explanation: Recall measures how many real positives were caught, so disease screening favours it. Precision matters more when acting on a false positive is expensive.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a confusion matrix?

options.text: It breaks predictions into true and false positives and negatives
It ranks features by importance
It measures training time per epoch
It shows correlation between features

questions.explanation: It shows which errors the model makes, not just how many. Precision, recall and specificity are all read off it, which a single accuracy figure hides.

questions.prompt: In pandas, what does groupby followed by agg do?

options.text: Removes rows with missing values
Joins two DataFrames on a key
Sorts rows by the grouping column
Splits rows into groups and computes a summary per group

questions.explanation: It follows split-apply-combine: partition by key, apply an aggregation, then assemble the results. It is the tabular equivalent of SQL's GROUP BY.

questions.prompt: Why should a time series be split chronologically rather than randomly?

options.text: Time series cannot be shuffled in pandas
Random splits are computationally slower
Chronological splits produce larger training sets
A random split lets the model train on the future

questions.explanation: Shuffling puts later observations into training, so the model sees the future it is meant to predict. Scores look excellent and collapse in deployment.

questions.prompt: What does correlation not imply?

options.text: That a linear relationship may exist
That one variable causes the other
That the relationship is measurable
That two variables move together

questions.explanation: A confounder can drive both variables, and the direction may be reversed. Establishing causation needs an experiment or a careful causal design.

questions.prompt: What is one-hot encoding used for?

options.text: Filling in missing values
Compressing numeric columns
Representing a categorical variable without implying an order
Scaling features to unit variance

questions.explanation: Encoding categories as 1, 2, 3 tells the model that 3 is greater than 1, which is false for colours or cities. One-hot avoids the fake ordering at the cost of extra columns.

questions.prompt: What is model drift?

options.text: Real-world data changing so a deployed model degrades
The model file becoming corrupted over time
Different results on repeated training runs
Gradual loss of numeric precision during training

questions.explanation: The world moves and the training distribution stops matching live data, so performance decays quietly. Monitoring inputs and outcomes after deployment is what catches it.

questions.prompt: Why should a baseline model be trained before a complex one?

options.text: It reduces the size of the dataset
It establishes whether the complexity actually buys anything
It guarantees the complex model will converge
It is required by scikit-learn's API

questions.explanation: Without a baseline there is no way to judge a score. A logistic regression that nearly matches a deep model usually wins on cost, latency and explainability.

questions.prompt: In an A/B test, what does statistical power describe?

options.text: The confidence that the null is true
The size of the observed effect
The proportion of users in the treatment group
The probability of detecting a real effect if one exists

questions.explanation: Power depends on sample size, effect size and variance. An underpowered test that shows no significance has not shown the feature does not work.

questions.prompt: What does a SQL window function let you do that GROUP BY does not?

options.text: Join more than two tables
Guarantee the result is sorted
Compute an aggregate while keeping each row
Filter rows before aggregation

questions.explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows; a window function computes over a partition and returns a value per row, which is how running totals and per-group ranks are produced.

questions.prompt: Why is dropping every row with a missing value often a poor choice?

options.text: Missing values always carry the strongest signal
Missingness is rarely random, so it biases what remains
Dropping rows changes the column data types
Most libraries cannot drop rows efficiently

questions.explanation: If a field is missing more often for one group, dropping those rows removes that group disproportionately. Missingness is sometimes informative enough to encode as a feature.

questions.prompt: What does feature scaling matter for?

options.text: Only for classification problems
Reducing the number of features
Distance-based and gradient-based algorithms
Decision trees and random forests

questions.explanation: kNN, SVMs and gradient descent are sensitive to feature magnitude, so an unscaled salary column dominates an age column. Tree splits are scale-invariant and unaffected.

questions.prompt: What is overfitting visible as during training?

options.text: Validation loss is always lower than training loss
Training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises
Both training and validation loss stay high
Training loss rises steadily

questions.explanation: The model is memorising training rows rather than learning generalisable structure. Early stopping halts at the point validation loss turns.

questions.prompt: Why is a random forest usually more robust than a single decision tree?

options.text: It cannot overfit at all
It trains on more data
Averaging many decorrelated trees reduces variance
It uses fewer features overall

questions.explanation: Each tree sees a bootstrap sample and a random feature subset, so their errors are partly independent and averaging cancels much of the variance.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?

options.text: Unsupervised learning needs more compute by definition
Supervised learning uses labelled targets; unsupervised does not
Supervised learning works only on images
Unsupervised learning cannot be evaluated at all

questions.explanation: Supervised learning fits a mapping to known answers. Unsupervised methods such as clustering find structure without labels, and are harder but not impossible to evaluate.

questions.prompt: Why is a chart's y-axis starting at a non-zero value sometimes misleading?

options.text: It exaggerates small differences visually
It hides the largest values
It breaks most plotting libraries
It changes the underlying data

questions.explanation: Truncating the axis magnifies a tiny change into a dramatic slope. It is legitimate when zero is not meaningful, but it must be obvious to the reader.

questions.prompt: What does a train-serve skew mean in a deployed ML system?

options.text: The serving hardware is slower than the training hardware
The model file differs between environments
Features are computed differently at training and inference
Training used a different random seed

questions.explanation: If a feature is computed one way in a training notebook and another way in the service, the model sees inputs it was never trained on. Sharing the transformation code removes it.
